prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Every, Because, Hispanics

outputs.L1:
My ocean town struggles to collect leaves, offer summer school, and keep our library open. Each day now, more men stand at the railroad station, waiting to be chosen for work. Because it is assumed that Hispanics will work for less, they are selected first, while the white and Black men avoid the terror in one another’s eyes.

Our handyman, Santos, who expects only what his hands earn, is proud of his half-acre in Guatemala, where he plans to retire. His desire to proceed with dignity is admirable, but he knows that now no one retires; everyone works harder. My father imagined a life more satisfying than the one he managed to lead. He did not see himself as uneducated, thwarted, or bitter, but as soon to be rich. Being rich, he believed, was his right. Happiness, I used to think, was a necessary illusion. Now I think it is only precious moments of relief, like dreams of Guatemala.

Sometimes, at night, in winter, surrounded by the significant silence of empty mansions—which once were cottages where people lived their lives, and now are owned by banks and the absent rich—I like to stand at my window, looking for a TV’s futile flickering, always surprised to see instead the quaint, porous face of my reflection, immersed in its one abundance.
outputs.L2:
My seaside town has trouble collecting fallen leaves, funding summer classes, and keeping the public library running. These days, more and more men gather daily at the train station, hoping someone will hire them. Since people assume Hispanic workers will accept lower pay, they are chosen first, while the white and Black men try not to meet the fear reflected in each other’s faces.

Our handyman, Santos, asks for nothing beyond what his own labor can earn. He takes pride in the half-acre he owns in Guatemala, the place where he hopes to spend his old age. His wish to move through life with dignity is deeply worthy of respect, though he understands that retirement has become impossible now; everyone simply has to work more. My father pictured a future richer and more fulfilling than the life he actually ended up living. He never thought of himself as poorly educated, blocked, or resentful; he thought of himself as someone on the verge of wealth. He felt being rich was something he deserved. I once believed happiness was an illusion people needed in order to go on. Now I think it consists only of rare, valuable intervals of ease, like visions of Guatemala.

On some winter nights, standing amid the heavy quiet of vacant mansions—houses that used to be modest cottages where people made their lives, but now belong to banks and wealthy owners who are never there—I stand by my window and search for the pointless flicker of a television. Instead, I am always startled to find the old-fashioned, vulnerable face of my own reflection, absorbed in the single plenty it possesses.
outputs.L3:
The town is increasingly overwhelmed, struggling to provide even the most basic services as more and more men gather at the railroad station each day, hoping to be chosen for work. Their waiting has become a symbol of desperation: men standing in line for a chance at wages, uncertain whether they will earn enough to support themselves or their families. The pressure on the town grows heavier as need increases and resources remain limited.

Among the workers, tension and fear continue to build. Hispanic men are often selected first because employers believe they will accept lower pay and work harder for less. This practice deepens resentment among the other workers, turning poverty into competition and dividing people who share the same struggle. Instead of seeing one another as allies, the men begin to view each other as threats to their survival.

Santos, the handyman, represents a quieter and more dignified response to hardship. He takes pride in earning his way, no matter how difficult the work may be. His labor is not only a means of survival but also a source of self-respect. What sustains him is his dream of returning to Guatemala, where he owns a half acre of land and imagines retiring with dignity. That small piece of land becomes a vision of peace, independence, and belonging.

The speaker reflects on the meaning of happiness through Santos’s dream. Perhaps happiness is not a permanent state or a grand illusion that can last forever. Instead, it may exist in brief moments of relief: the comfort of imagining home, the hope of rest after years of labor, or the belief that one’s efforts will eventually lead somewhere. Santos’s dream of Guatemala becomes one of those moments, fragile but deeply meaningful.

At night, the speaker observes another side of the town: large mansions standing empty, owned by banks or absent wealthy people who rarely, if ever, appear. These houses represent abundance without life, wealth without presence. Looking at them, the speaker feels both the loneliness of such emptiness and the strange excess reflected back from their dark windows. In a place where so many people wait for work and struggle to survive, the unused mansions become a haunting image of inequality, isolation, and wasted plenty.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents an ocean town marked by economic decline, where everyday life is shaped by scarcity, competition, and uncertainty. The setting is not romanticized as a peaceful seaside place; instead, the ocean town becomes a landscape of worn-down public services, limited work, and people struggling to maintain dignity under difficult conditions. Public spaces and institutions seem strained, suggesting a community that has been neglected or left behind. Against this backdrop, day laborers compete for temporary jobs, revealing how poverty turns survival into a contest among people who share similar hardships.

Immigrant experience is central to the poem’s vision of the town. The poem shows immigrants not as distant figures, but as people carrying burdens of displacement, labor, and hope. Their hardship is tied to the larger economic collapse around them, yet it is also personal: they must endure insecurity while trying to build lives for themselves and their families. Family aspirations remain important, especially the desire for children to have better futures. These hopes give the poem emotional depth, because they show that even in a damaged social world, people continue to dream, work, and care for one another.

The speaker observes these conditions with a reflective and often sorrowful awareness. Rather than offering a simple political argument, the poem gathers details of ordinary life and lets them reveal the town’s inequality. The speaker notices both the visible signs of poverty and the quieter forms of dispossession: lost opportunities, exhausted workers, and communities forced to accept less than they deserve. The poem’s power comes from this attention to small moments, where larger social problems become intimate and human.

Yet the poem does not portray life as entirely empty of joy. Happiness and dignity still appear, but only briefly and fragilely. They survive in fleeting moments of beauty, affection, pride, or shared endurance. These small consolations matter deeply because they allow people to feel human in a world that often treats them as disposable. At the same time, the poem makes clear that such moments are not enough to overcome the larger forces of inequality and deprivation. The result is a bittersweet vision: the poem honors the preciousness of brief happiness while also recognizing its insufficiency in the face of economic hardship and social injustice.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the voice of an older resident of a struggling seaside town during an economic downturn, reflecting on unemployment, immigration, class resentment, family disappointment, and the meaning of happiness.
counterfactuals.output:
At the bus shelter  
where the Perspex is cracked  
and the timetable is more wish  
than promise,  
I watch the gulls fight over chips  
like they’ve read the papers  
and know there’s less to go round.

This town used to wake early.  
Men with lunch tins, women with hair pinned back,  
boots on the pavement,  
the harbor clanking like a drawer of cutlery.  
You could tell the hour  
by the factory horn,  
by the shift changing,  
by the smell of diesel and bread.

Now the factory is flats  
no one here can afford,  
all glass balconies facing the gray,  
and the job centre opens at nine  
to a queue of lads  
who once would have been too proud  
to stand still that long.

My son says there’s nothing here for him.  
He says it like I built the place myself  
and let it rot on purpose.  
He lives inland now,  
near a ring road and a retail park,  
sends photographs of the children  
holding plastic buckets on beaches in Spain.  
They have my eyes, I think,  
though they would not know my street  
if you set them down at the corner.

There are new voices in the shops,  
new names over the old cafés,  
spices where there used to be vinegar,  
men sending money home  
from wages too small  
to keep a coat decent.  
Some in the pub blame them.  
Some blame London.  
Some blame the ones on benefits,  
the ones in suits,  
the ones with brown faces,  
the ones with second homes,  
the ones with none.

I have blamed them too,  
on bitter nights  
when the meter took its bite  
and the sea wind came through the frames.  
Anger is easy to carry.  
It fits the hand  
like a stone.

But I have seen the young mother  
from three doors down  
walk her boy to school in the rain,  
her shoes letting in water.  
I have seen the old banker  
from the hill  
step over a sleeping man  
as if poverty were weather.  
I have seen my own face  
in the dark window of the off-license,  
looking for someone to accuse.

Class, they used to say,  
was knowing your place.  
Mine was a rented terrace,  
a Friday envelope,  
a holiday week if the boiler held out.  
The rich had curtains that never twitched  
and gardens facing away from the town.  
Now even resentment has been priced up,  
sold back to us on television  
by men with polished teeth  
who have never missed a meal.

What did I want for my children?  
Not riches.  
Not really.  
A steady wage.  
A door they could paint any color.  
Someone to come home to.  
A reason to put the kettle on  
without feeling foolish.

My daughter does not call much.  
She says I am hard work.  
Perhaps I am.  
I saved all my tenderness  
for emergencies  
and then wondered  
why no one came looking for it.

The sea keeps arriving,  
which is something.  
Morning after morning  
it lays its cold hand  
on the shore  
and takes back the footprints.  
The pier is rusting,  
the arcade half-empty,  
the hotel sign missing two letters,  
but the light still breaks  
on the water sometimes  
so suddenly  
you forgive the whole world  
for a minute.

Maybe happiness was never  
the brass band version,  
never the prize house,  
the full wallet,  
the children staying close.  
Maybe it is smaller  
and more stubborn:

a warm room,  
a clean shirt,  
a neighbor’s nod,  
the first mackerel flashing silver  
in a borrowed bucket,  
the courage to stop naming enemies  
and start counting losses honestly.

At dusk  
I sit on the sea wall  
with my bad knee and my paper cup of tea.  
The gulls scream overhead,  
greedy as kings,  
and the tide comes in  
over the black rocks,  
covering everything  
for a while  
with the same shining water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary prose-poem about an ocean town where municipal services are failing, day laborers wait by the railroad station, a Guatemalan handyman dreams of retirement, and empty mansions owned by banks surround the speaker.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the ocean town exhales through its storm drains, a briny breath and then a cough. The streetlights blink all morning, confused by fog. The trash is not collected. The library doors are chained with a notice fading in the salt air. At city hall, a fern dies in the window beside a sign promising renewal, while gulls wheel over the parking meters as if over a battlefield no one will name.

By the railroad station the day laborers gather in jackets too thin for the wind. They stand with their hands around coffee, watching each truck slow and decide. Their faces lift briefly, then lower. The tracks shine with a cold intelligence. Somewhere beyond the platforms, the sea repeats itself, tireless, but here time comes in hourly wages, in the squeal of brakes, in the foreman’s finger counting bodies.

Among them is Mateo, from Guatemala, who fixes whatever the town breaks and refuses to mend: buckled steps, burst pipes, fences slumped like old horses. He can coax a furnace into flame, replace a lock, patch a roof before rain. In the evenings he tells me he dreams of retirement—not beaches, not golf, but a small house inland where tomatoes redden against a wall, where his knees do not ache, where no one calls at midnight because water is pouring through a ceiling owned by nobody and everyone.

The mansions around me are empty, though their lawns are cut by machines that arrive like insects and depart before noon. Banks own the columns, the widows’ walks, the marble kitchens where dust lies gently on granite. At night their windows mirror the moon, blind and immaculate. I live among these shells, these foreclosed palaces, listening to pipes knock in houses without sleepers, alarms crying for absent masters, the surf making its old argument with the shore.

We are all waiting here: the men by the station, the unpaid bills in municipal drawers, the boarded arcade, the police cruiser idling without gas money, Mateo with his tool belt and his orchard in the mind. Even the ocean seems to wait, drawing back each wave as if reconsidering the town, then returning, returning, to erase our footprints with a tenderness that feels almost like neglect.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a somber, socially conscious poem in a style reminiscent of contemporary American confessional poetry, touching on recession, race, immigrant labor, a father’s failed dreams of wealth, and a speaker looking at their reflection at night.
counterfactuals.output:
At midnight the bathroom mirror  
holds my face like a debt  
no one intends to forgive.

The light above it flickers—  
small recession in the glass—  
and I see my father behind me,  
not as a ghost, but as a man  
counting tips on the kitchen table,  
his thumbs dark with newspaper ink,  
his mouth practicing English  
for customers who never learned  
to say his name.

He came here believing money  
was a country you could enter  
if you worked long enough,  
if you swallowed the insult,  
if you let your back become  
a bridge for other people’s luggage.  
He washed dishes, swept floors,  
stood in the cold outside buildings  
where men in clean coats  
spoke of markets as if they were weather,  
as if no one had made the storm.

Then the factories closed.  
Then the houses emptied.  
Then the bank took its slow, white hand  
and pressed it over the town’s mouth.  
On the news, men said downturn  
like it was a season,  
not a family eating rice for dinner  
three nights in a row,  
not my mother cutting coupons  
with the seriousness of surgery,  
not Black boys stopped on corners  
for resembling a fear  
someone else had inherited.

My father wanted wealth  
the way a thirsty man wants rain.  
Not yachts, not gold—  
just a door that opened  
without asking who he was,  
a bill paid before it turned red,  
a Sunday suit that did not smell  
of someone else’s grease.

But America kept moving  
the finish line down the road.  
It called him essential  
when it needed his hands,  
illegal when it needed a reason  
not to pay him.  
It praised his hunger,  
then blamed him for eating.

Now I stand here grown,  
face divided by the mirror’s seam,  
one half shadow, one half tired light,  
and I wonder what part of me  
is mine.

Outside, sirens braid the dark.  
Somewhere a woman boards a bus  
before dawn to clean an office  
where her picture will never hang.  
Somewhere a man folds his last paycheck  
into a wallet thin as prayer.  
Somewhere a child translates a landlord’s notice  
and learns how shame sounds  
in two languages.

I rinse my face.  
The water runs clear, then not.  
I look again and see  
my father’s failed kingdom:  
a rented room, a cracked plate,  
the stubborn republic of his hands.

I want to forgive him  
for dreaming in dollars,  
for teaching me hope  
as a kind of labor.

But the mirror gives back only this—  
my own eyes, open late,  
asking what survives  
when the dream is repossessed,  
and who among us  
was ever meant to wake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person meditation set in a coastal town after the housing crash, including details about leaf pickup, summer school, a library, men seeking work at the train station, and the silence of vacant mansions.
counterfactuals.output:
After the crash, the town seemed to exhale and never quite breathe in again.

I remember the leaf pickup that autumn: the notices stapled to telephone poles, the schedule printed in the weekly paper, the long brown windrows raked to the curb in front of houses no one lived in anymore. The town trucks came groaning through the streets, their orange lights turning in the mist, sucking up leaves with a hose like some enormous animal feeding. In other years there had been children jumping into those piles, fathers calling from driveways, dogs nosing through the damp gold. That year the leaves lay undisturbed outside the empty colonials and shingled summer houses, gathering rain, flattening into the gutters. The crews came anyway. The town kept its routines. It collected what had fallen.

I was teaching summer school then, though “summer” felt like a technicality. The mornings began with a marine layer that dulled the ocean and made the playground smell of wet metal and cut grass. My students came in sleepy, embarrassed to be there, carrying pencils in their fists and the heaviness of households where adults spoke in lowered voices. We read short stories under fluorescent lights while gulls cried over the roof. Sometimes, in the middle of a sentence, I would look up and see the beach traffic moving beyond the school windows—contractors’ trucks, a realtor’s car, a bank van—and feel that we were all repeating lessons we had failed to learn the first time.

In the afternoons I went to the library.

It was one of the few places that still felt public in the old sense: heated in winter, cool in summer, patient with everyone. The unemployed sat at the computers filling out applications for jobs that would never call back. Mothers whispered to children in the picture-book room. Retirees read newspapers from wooden poles, though the news had become a weather system no one could escape. I used to sit near the window with a stack of returned books and watch the harbor road, the slow drift of people who had nowhere urgent to be. The librarians lowered their voices as if tending a sickroom. They stamped due dates. They answered questions. They kept lending.

At the train station, men gathered before dawn.

Some had tool belts in their hands, some had lunch coolers, some wore boots whitened with old plaster dust. They stood in small groups on the platform, looking not toward the city-bound train but toward the parking lot, waiting for contractors who might need an extra body for the day. There was a way they held themselves—ready, but not hopeful. A pickup would pull in and a few men would step forward. A window would roll down. A name might be called, or a hand might gesture. Then the truck would leave, and the others would remain beneath the gull-streaked shelter, sipping coffee, staring down the tracks.

I passed them on my way to school and felt a shame I could not place. I had work, though not enough. I had a room, though the rent rose even as the houses around me emptied. I had books to assign, papers to grade, a key to the building. They had skills that had built the town’s visible wealth—its decks and slate roofs, its kitchens faced in marble, its cedar shingles left to silver in salt air—and now the wealth had withdrawn behind notices, locks, and overgrown hedges.

The vacant mansions were the quietest part.

They stood along the bluff roads with their ocean views and darkened windows, their security signs planted in the lawns like small flags of surrender. Some had Adirondack chairs still arranged toward the water, as if the family had just gone inside for lemonade and would return any minute. Others had blue tarps over sections of roof, copper gutters stolen, pools filmed green beneath covers sagging with rain. The driveways filled with pine needles. Newspapers yellowed in their plastic sleeves. At night, whole stretches of shoreline road were unlit, the houses facing the sea like blind faces.

I used to walk there after dinner when the air smelled of kelp and honeysuckle and diesel from the fishing boats. My footsteps sounded too loud. The ocean kept moving with its old indifference, shouldering itself against the rocks, dragging back pebbles with a hiss. I would stop in front of one mansion or another and imagine the silence inside: empty refrigerators, thermostats turned low, staircases no one climbed, guest rooms made up for guests who would not come. It was not a peaceful silence. It was the silence of stopped clocks, of bills unopened, of lives abruptly packed into boxes or left behind entirely.

And yet the town went on pretending to be seasonal.

Flags appeared for Memorial Day. The ice-cream stand opened. The high school announced summer enrichment and credit recovery. The library posted a reading challenge with paper whales in the children’s room. Leaf pickup came around again when the maples burned red and the oaks let go. People learned to speak in euphemisms: underwater, short sale, restructuring, between things. We said “after the crash” the way people in other places said “after the storm,” though no roofs had been torn off by wind, no boats thrown into streets. What had broken was less visible and everywhere.

I think now that I was learning to listen to vacancy.

Not emptiness exactly, because nothing was empty. The houses were full of absence. The station was full of waiting. The library was full of need. My classroom was full of children absorbing the tremors of adult failure while conjugating verbs and reducing fractions. Even the leaf piles at the curb seemed to contain a message: that whatever we built, borrowed, promised, or named our own would eventually come loose and have to be gathered.

I stayed in that coastal town longer than I expected. Long enough to see some mansions bought at auction and lit again, long enough to see others torn down for new ones larger than before. Long enough for my summer school students to graduate, or not, and for the men at the station to thin out as work returned in uneven patches. But whenever autumn comes, wherever I am, I think of those municipal trucks moving through the salt-gray morning, collecting leaves from in front of vacant houses with the same impartial care they gave to occupied ones.

That, more than anything, is how I remember the town after the crash: the ocean speaking, the library glowing, men waiting for work before sunrise, children bent over their summer lessons, and the great houses on the hill holding their breath in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a bleak lyrical monologue about economic inequality and fragile hope, featuring a handyman named Santos from Guatemala, the speaker’s father who believed he deserved to be rich, and an ending with the speaker seeing their own reflection in a dark window.
counterfactuals.output:
Santos came from Guatemala with a toolbox  
and a back that seemed already mortgaged to the world.  
He fixed what other people broke:  
hinges, gutters, the sour mouths of drains,  
the loose teeth of old staircases,  
the wires that sparked like tiny rebellions in the walls.  

He arrived before sunrise in a van the color of dust,  
ate lunch from foil on the curb,  
and called every man “boss”  
as if the word were a coin he could not afford to drop.  

My father liked him.  
My father liked anyone who worked hard  
because he believed work was a staircase  
and not, as Santos knew, a wheel.  

My father believed he deserved to be rich.  
Not wanted—deserved.  
As though somewhere, in a locked room,  
there was a ledger with his name in gold,  
a clerical error keeping him from the house on the hill,  
the car that hummed like a satisfied animal,  
the watch bright enough to silence shame.  

He would stand in our kitchen at night  
with the refrigerator buzzing behind him,  
talking about men stupider than him  
who had boats, who had second homes,  
who shook hands and inherited weather.  
He said the world owed him.  
He said it with such sorrow  
it almost sounded true.  

And Santos, who patched our roof after the first hard rain,  
who carried ladders like crosses,  
who sent money south in envelopes thin as prayers,  
only smiled when my father spoke this way.  
A small smile.  
Not cruel.  
Not kind.  
The smile of a man who has seen  
how many forms hunger can take.  

There are people born holding keys.  
There are people born outside the building.  
There are people hired to repair the locks.  

I learned this slowly,  
watching my father curse the bills,  
watching Santos count cash with cracked fingers,  
watching the rich houses glow above town  
like ships refusing rescue.  

Still, hope came sometimes—  
weak, ridiculous, persistent.  
A weed in the seam of the sidewalk.  
A light left on in a room nobody owned.  
Santos humming while he worked.  
My father buying a lottery ticket  
and folding it carefully into his wallet  
like a photograph of a child.  

I did not know which was sadder:  
to believe you were meant for more  
or to know exactly what you would be given.  

Years later, I pass dark storefronts  
where mannequins wear clothes worth more than rent,  
and the city shines its cold coins under my feet.  
I think of Santos, somewhere under another roof.  
I think of my father, still arguing his case  
before a judge who never appears.  

And in the black window of a closed bank,  
between the advertisements for futures  
no one I know can afford,  
I see my own face looking back—  
pale, divided, waiting—  
as if I too have been standing there for years,  
outside the glass,  
mistaking my reflection for a door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
